chunks: "The difference is the type of carrier that forms the channel.
An N-channel MOSFET sits in a p-type body with n+ source and drain, and when I put a positive voltage on the gate it pulls electrons to the surface and inverts a thin layer into n-type.
That is the channel. A P-channel device is the mirror image: n-type body, p+ source and drain, and a negative gate-to-source voltage pulls holes up to form the channel.
So the voltages flip. An NMOS turns on when the gate is higher than the source by more than V t , around 1 volts, and its source usually sits at ground.
A PMOS turns on when the gate is lower than the source by more than V t , and its source usually sits at the supply. The other practical difference is mobility.
Electrons are about two to three times more mobile than holes, so for the same W/L an NMOS has about 2. 5 times the current and a lower on-resistance.
To match them you make the PMOS wider, which costs area and gate capacitance.
That's why you see NMOS used wherever you have a choice, and PMOS where it makes the gate drive simple, like a high-side load switch or the pull-up half of a CMOS inverter."
